captions.text: IC gives incident commanders, command aides and supervisors a
shared place to review an incident.
Begin in Calls.
The visible cards identify the Vehicle rescue exercise as DEMO zero zero
zero three, and the Community medical standby as DEMO zero zero zero two.
Each card brings together its name, location and assigned resources.
Read those details together before selecting the incident
you intend to review.
Search calls is above the list when you need to locate another incident.

scenes.title: Confirm the selected call and command context

captions.text: For the detailed review, we use the separate Warehouse alarm
exercise, DEMO zero zero zero one.
Call Details shows that name and number at the top.
Its description says reported smoke at an unoccupied training warehouse, with Squad

captions.text: Active Command and Open Command Board are visible on the right.
Confirm the selected incident before carrying information into a command
board; a similar exercise name in the list can refer to a different call.

scenes.title: Check the stored incident location and reference tools

captions.text: Immediately below the incident description, the map shows the
training incident pin in Chicago.
The location label reads Training site one, fictional, Chicago, Illinois.

spoken_references.Training site 1 (fictional), Chicago, IL: Training site one, fictional, Chicago, Illinois

captions.text: Compare that stored location with the incident you are reviewing.
It is incident context; it is not evidence of a responder arriving there.
Notes, Images, Files and Route sit together below the map.
Identify these entry points so you know where to look for supporting information
when coordinating with another operator.

scenes.title: Read the complete Readiness result

captions.text: Scroll to the call tabs and choose Readiness.
The selected tab is underlined.
In this exercise, the unit row names Squad Three and shows Ready on the right.
Read the next line as well: No completed checks in this window.
required_labels: No completed checks in this window.

No completed checks in this window

captions.text: Those two messages are visible together.
The Ready label alone does not establish that someone
completed an apparatus checklist.
During a handover, report the unit name, the displayed status and
the evidence message together.
That helps the next operator identify what still needs confirmation.

visual_required_labels: No completed checks in this window.

captions.text: Choose Check-In at the right end of the same tab row.
In this exercise, the selected tab says No check-in timers active.
That is the current result for this call.
It does not show a completed personnel check-in or an accountability result.
Keep this observation separate from the unit readiness summary.
An operator who only reports Ready has omitted the fact that this call view
currently has no active check-in timers.

scenes.title: Compare both views before a handover

captions.text: Compare the two tabs before briefing a relief operator.
Readiness shows Squad Three as Ready, with no completed checks in this window.
required_labels: No completed checks in this window.

no completed checks in this window

captions.text: Check-In shows no active timers.
A useful handover preserves both statements, instead of turning either one
into a blanket assurance about the crew.
Resolve missing operational information through your
department's coordination process.
In practice, read each tab aloud and have a colleague identify which
facts were actually displayed.

visual_required_labels: No completed checks in this window.

scenes.title: Carry the verified context into command coordination

captions.text: Return to the call heading to confirm the incident identity again before
moving on to Open Command Board.
The same review pattern helps a fire or E M S command aide, a community
paramedicine or mental health coordinator, a search-and-rescue lead, a security
supervisor, a wildland contractor or an industrial response team.
Names and assignments will differ, but the task is the same: identify
the incident, read the actual status and evidence messages, then pass on a
precise account of what the screens show.
